questions.question_text: A distribution of household incomes is strongly skewed right. Which is the best measure of center?
questions.option_a: Mean, because it uses every data value
questions.option_b: Median, because it resists the pull of extreme values
questions.explanation: Right skew drags the mean above the typical value; the median resists outliers. 'Uses every value' is exactly why the mean fails here — high earners inflate it. Range isn't even a measure of center.

questions.question_text: If every value in a data set is increased by 10, what happens to the mean and standard deviation?
questions.option_b: Mean increases by 10; standard deviation is unchanged
questions.option_c: Mean is unchanged; standard deviation increases by 10
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts location (mean, median) but doesn't change spread — every point moves together, so distances between points are identical. Multiplying is what changes the SD.

questions.question_text: A study finds r = 0.92 between ice cream sales and drowning deaths. The best interpretation is:
questions.option_b: There is a strong positive linear association, likely explained by a lurking variable such as temperature
questions.option_c: The correlation is too high to be real
questions.option_d: 92% of drownings are explained by ice cream sales
questions.explanation: Correlation ≠ causation; hot weather drives both variables. Option D confuses r with r² — and even r² = 0.85 means 'variation explained,' never 'caused.' This lurking-variable setup appears on nearly every exam.

questions.question_text: A least-squares regression line is ŷ = 12 + 3.5x. The residual for a point (2, 21) is:
questions.explanation: Predicted: ŷ = 12 + 3.5(2) = 19. Residual = actual − predicted = 21 − 19 = 2. The sign convention matters: positive residual means the point sits above the line. Reversing the subtraction gives −2.

questions.question_text: A radio host asks listeners to call in about a tax proposal. This sampling method suffers most from:
questions.explanation: Call-in polls attract people with strong opinions — the sample selects itself. Nonresponse bias is different: it happens when people chosen for a sample fail to respond. The distinction between these two is a frequent multiple-choice trap.

questions.question_text: Why does random assignment in an experiment allow cause-and-effect conclusions?
questions.option_a: It guarantees the sample represents the population
questions.option_b: It balances lurking variables across treatment groups on average
questions.option_c: It eliminates all variability in responses
questions.option_d: It ensures the placebo effect is removed
questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads confounders evenly between groups, so treatment is the only systematic difference. Representing the population is random SELECTION's job (generalization), not random assignment's — keep the two random's separate.

questions.question_text: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
questions.option_a: Yes, because P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B)
questions.option_c: No, because A and B can occur together
questions.explanation: Independence check: P(A)·P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 = P(A and B) ✓. Options B and C confuse independent with mutually exclusive — mutually exclusive events (with nonzero probabilities) are never independent.

questions.question_text: X has mean 10 and SD 2; Y has mean 5 and SD 1.5. If X and Y are independent, the standard deviation of X − Y is:
questions.explanation: Variances ADD even when subtracting: Var(X−Y) = 4 + 2.25 = 6.25, so SD = 2.5. Subtracting SDs (0.5) is the classic error — spread increases whenever you combine independent sources of variability. D is the variance, not the SD.

questions.question_text: Which scenario satisfies all conditions of a binomial setting?
questions.option_a: Drawing 5 cards from a deck without replacement and counting hearts
questions.option_b: Flipping a fair coin 20 times and counting heads
questions.option_c: Rolling a die until the first 6 appears
questions.option_d: Measuring the height of 30 random students
questions.explanation: Binomial = fixed n, independent trials, same p, counting successes (BINS). Drawing without replacement breaks independence; 'until first success' is geometric; height is continuous, not a count.

questions.question_text: A population is strongly skewed with mean 50 and SD 12. For random samples of size 36, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately:
questions.explanation: CLT: n = 36 ≥ 30, so x̄ is approximately normal regardless of population shape, with SD = σ/√n = 12/6 = 2. Forgetting to divide by √n (option B) is the most common error on this topic.

questions.question_text: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is (24.3, 28.7). Which interpretation is correct?
questions.option_a: 95% of the data lie between 24.3 and 28.7
questions.option_b: There is a 95% probability the true mean is between 24.3 and 28.7
questions.option_c: We are 95% confident the interval (24.3, 28.7) captures the true population mean
questions.option_d: 95% of sample means fall in this interval
questions.explanation: Confidence is in the METHOD: 95% of intervals built this way capture μ. Option B treats μ as random — but μ is fixed; the interval is what varies. This wording distinction is worth a point on nearly every FRQ.

questions.question_text: A test of H₀: p = 0.5 vs Hₐ: p > 0.5 yields P-value 0.03. At α = 0.05, the correct conclusion is:
questions.option_a: Accept H₀ — the coin is fair
questions.option_b: Reject H₀ — there is convincing evidence that p > 0.5
questions.option_c: Reject Hₐ — the result is due to chance
questions.option_d: The probability H₀ is true is 0.03
questions.explanation: P-value 0.03 < α = 0.05 → reject H₀ in favor of Hₐ. We never 'accept' H₀ (only fail to reject), and the P-value is P(data this extreme | H₀ true) — not the probability H₀ is true. Both phrasings in A and D lose credit.

questions.question_text: A medical test screens for a disease with H₀: patient is healthy. A Type II error means:
questions.option_a: Telling a healthy patient they have the disease
questions.option_b: Telling a sick patient they are healthy
questions.option_d: Running the test at too small an α
questions.explanation: Type II = failing to reject H₀ when it's false = missing the disease. Type I (option A) is the false alarm. Mnemonic: Type I = crying wolf, Type II = missing the wolf. Consequences differ — here a Type II is far more dangerous.

questions.question_text: Which change increases the power of a significance test?
questions.option_d: Using a two-sided test instead of one-sided
questions.explanation: Larger n shrinks sampling variability, making real effects easier to detect. Lowering α makes rejecting harder (less power); two-sided tests split α across tails (less power for a given direction). Power ↑ with n, α, and effect size.

questions.question_text: A chi-square test of independence on a 3×4 two-way table has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6. Option A is the cell count, option B is cells − 1 (which is the df for a goodness-of-fit test with 12 categories — a different test).

questions.question_text: When should you use a t-distribution instead of z for inference about a mean?
questions.option_a: When the sample size is large
questions.option_b: When the population standard deviation is unknown
questions.option_c: When the population is not normal
questions.explanation: t replaces z whenever σ is estimated by s — which is nearly always in practice. The extra uncertainty from estimating σ is exactly what t's heavier tails account for. Sample size affects degrees of freedom, not the z-vs-t choice.

questions.question_text: Researchers measure cholesterol before and after a diet on the same 40 subjects. The appropriate test is:
questions.explanation: Before/after on the same subjects = paired data — analyze the 40 differences as one sample. A two-sample t-test wrongly assumes the groups are independent, throwing away the pairing and inflating variability.

questions.question_text: SAT scores are N(1050, 200). Approximately what proportion of students score above 1250?
questions.explanation: 1250 is one SD above the mean. By the empirical rule, 68% lie within ±1 SD, leaving 32% in the two tails — 16% in the upper tail. Option A forgets to halve; option D reads the middle instead of the tail.

questions.question_text: Computer output for a regression shows slope b = 2.8 with SE = 0.9 based on n = 25 points. The t-statistic for testing H₀: β = 0 is approximately:
questions.explanation: t = (b − 0)/SE = 2.8/0.9 ≈ 3.11 with df = n − 2 = 23. Option C inverts the ratio; option D is a critical value, not a test statistic. Reading regression output is a guaranteed exam item — know which number is which.

questions.question_text: A basketball player makes 80% of free throws. The probability that her first miss occurs on the 3rd attempt is:
questions.explanation: First miss on attempt 3 = make, make, miss = (0.8)(0.8)(0.2). This is geometric — exact sequence, no counting coefficient. Option D adds a binomial coefficient, which belongs to 'exactly one miss in 3 attempts,' a different question.
